subsection: 2. Selecting a large and a small household appliance

notes.h: Selection criteria: cost, size and capacity
notes.b: Before buying, compare the cost, size and capacity of each model against what the household needs. A good choice is value for money, which means quality against price, not simply the lowest price.
points: Initial cost: compare the purchase price, including delivery and installation, across several shops and brands, so you know the true cost of getting the appliance working in your home.
Running cost: this is the energy and water the appliance uses over its life. Compare it with the purchase price, since a cheap appliance can cost more to run, and the energy label shows this.
Size and space: the appliance must fit the available space and allow room for doors to open, air to circulate (ventilation) and access to plumbing and power points.
Capacity: match it to household size, such as litres of fresh and frozen food for a fridge or kilograms of laundry for a washing machine, and litres for a kettle.
Payment method: compare cash, debit or credit card and credit agreements, and the total amount payable under any credit, because credit adds to the final cost.
notes.tip: Outline three factors for selecting an appliance, and give each factor a clause saying why it matters, for example that running cost can outweigh a low purchase price.

notes.h: Selection criteria: reliability, aftercare and ease of use
notes.b: Cost and size are not the whole story. A buyer also checks how long the appliance will last, who will fix it, and how easy and safe it is to use every day.
points: Brand reputation and reliability: established brands with a record of durable products, good reviews and available spare parts are less likely to need early repair.
Guarantee and after-sales service: check the length of the guarantee, what it covers, and how quickly repairs, servicing, spare parts, delivery and installation are available.
Ease of operation and cleaning: clear controls, removable parts and filters, smooth surfaces, dishwasher-safe parts and cord storage reduce the time and effort of use.
Safety features: automatic cut-outs, interlocks, child lock, cool-touch surfaces and recognised safety marks reduce the risk of injury or fire.
Family needs and modern features: choose features the household will actually use, such as programmes, timers and smart controls, rather than paying for extras that stay unused.
notes.tip: Link each factor to a reason when you answer, for example that a long guarantee and available spare parts protect you from the cost of repair.

notes.b: The same criteria apply to every appliance, but how much each one matters depends on the size and price of what you are buying. Apply them to one large and one small example.
points: Large appliances (cooker, fridge, washing machine, dishwasher, tumble dryer) are expensive and long-lived and usually delivered and installed, so cost, energy efficiency, size and servicing weigh most.
Small appliances (kettle, toaster, iron, food processor, mixer) are cheaper and portable, so storage, cleaning and cord length weigh more.
Examples to use for the individual studies: a washing machine, fridge-freezer or dishwasher as the large appliance, and a kettle, toaster, food processor or iron as the small one.

notes.b: Design is how an appliance looks and works, and construction is what it is made of and how well it is built. Together they decide how safe, durable and easy to clean it is.
points: Design affects safety, durability, ease of use and cleaning, and how well the appliance fits the style and colour of the kitchen.
Controls should be clearly labelled, easy to reach and simple to read; large, simple controls suit older users and children.
Weight, handles and grip should suit the person using the appliance, so that lifting and pouring are safe, and non-slip feet give stability.

Robust construction and good-quality materials, such as stainless steel for surfaces and blades, increase durability. Other materials used include heat-resistant or cool-touch plastic, glass and enamelled steel.
Smooth, sealed surfaces and removable parts are easier to clean and give fewer places for food and bacteria to collect. Sealed joints and a strong flex and plug add durability.
Design for safety and efficiency: insulation, interlocks, automatic cut-off, energy-saving settings and quiet running make the appliance safer and cheaper to use.
Examples of safe design: an interlock stops a machine working while its door is open, so fingers cannot reach moving parts.

notes.h: Energy efficiency and the EU energy label
notes.b: The energy label lets buyers compare the energy efficiency of appliances at a glance, on a common scale. An efficient appliance costs less to run and does less harm to the environment.
points: The EU energy label rates an appliance from A to G, where A is the most efficient and G the least efficient. This scale applies to fridges, freezers, washing machines, washer-dryers and dishwashers from 1 March 2021, and to tumble dryers from 1 July 2025.

The label is displayed on refrigerating appliances (fridges, freezers and fridge-freezers), washing machines, washer-dryers, dishwashers and tumble dryers. Two named appliances are enough if asked to name two.
A-rated appliances use the least electricity, so they cost least to run and cause the least harm to the environment; G-rated appliances use the most.
The label gives annual energy consumption in kilowatt-hours (kWh), which indicates likely running cost and environmental impact. Washing machine and dishwasher labels give energy per 100 cycles.
It also gives, depending on the appliance, the noise level in decibels, capacity and water use. A refrigeration label shows the fresh and frozen capacity in litres.
The current label carries a QR code that links to the product's entry in the EU product database (EPREL) for more detail.
Energy in kWh equals power in kW multiplied by hours used. Higher Level answers can use this to compare the running costs of two appliances.
Efficiency in use is also the consumer's job: use full loads, eco programmes and lower temperatures, switch off standby, and choose the correct size.
notes.tip: Say what the label is for (comparing efficiency at a glance, for lower running cost and less environmental harm), give the scale direction (A best), and name two appliances that carry it. For 6 marks give two linked points.

notes.b: A star rating on a fridge-freezer or freezer tells you how cold the frozen-food compartment is and how long frozen food keeps in it.
points: The star rating applies to the frozen-food compartment of fridges and fridge-freezers and to freezers, not to the fresh-food section.
One star: the compartment holds frozen food at −6°C for up to one week.
Two stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −12°C for up to one month.
Three stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −18°C for up to three months.
Four stars: the compartment holds frozen food at −18°C to −25°C for up to one year, and fresh food can be frozen in it. Only four stars allows this.
The star rating measures storage performance, not energy efficiency, so the energy label is used to compare running costs.
notes.tip: Give all four ratings with temperature and storage time, and say that fresh food can be frozen only at four stars. Remember that star ratings never apply to the fresh-food section, and a four-star compartment does not mean the most efficient appliance.

notes.b: Marks on an appliance or its packaging tell the buyer that a standard has been met. Each mark means something different, so know what each one does and does not show.
points: The CE mark is the manufacturer's declaration that the product meets the health, safety and environmental requirements of the European Union. It is not independent testing.

The double insulation symbol, a square inside a square, shows that the appliance has two layers of insulation (a Class II appliance), so it needs no earth wire and its plug has no earth connection. It is common on plastic-bodied small appliances.
The Irish Standard mark of the National Standards Authority of Ireland (NSAI) shows that the product has been certified to a standard.
An ISO 9000 quality mark shows that the maker's quality-management system has been assessed.
Marks should appear on the appliance or its packaging, and a mark that cannot be found on the product does not show certification.
Safety marks show that a product has been tested to a standard, but they do not guarantee its performance or reliability.
A manufacturer's guarantee or a retailer's own-brand label is not an independent mark.
notes.tip: State what a named mark tells the consumer: CE for European safety standards, double insulation for two layers of insulation and no earth, ISO 9000 for the maker's quality system. Do not call CE a quality mark awarded after independent testing.

notes.b: Before buying, a consumer gathers information from several sources. Some are independent, some come from sellers and may be biased, and some are personal experience.
points: Independent sources: consumer magazines and websites that test and compare products publish independent results on appliance models.
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC), the body for consumer protection and information, publishes guidance for consumers on their rights when buying appliances.

Citizens Information offers free, independent information on consumer rights and on buying goods and services. The European Consumer Centre Ireland helps with cross-border purchases, and libraries also hold information.
Manufacturers' leaflets and brochures give specifications, guidelines for use and guarantee terms, but they are promotional documents.
Product labels and packaging show the energy rating, safety marks, capacity and guarantee details, so you can compare models for example in the shop.
Sales staff can explain features, but their advice may be influenced by the stock and margins of the shop. Advertisements highlight strengths, so check their claims against independent sources.
Word of mouth, online user reviews and in-shop demonstrations reflect other people's experience; read them critically because they can be unreliable.

Benefits of getting information before buying: compare price, installation and running cost; find the most energy-efficient model; compare features, design, size and ease of operation; reduce the influence of advertising; avoid a costly mistake.
notes.tip: Name two or three sources, say what each offers and give one limit, for example that a manufacturer's leaflet is promotional. Be ready to give the benefits of getting information before buying.

notes.h: Environmentally responsible choice, use and disposal
notes.b: An appliance affects the environment at three points: when it is chosen, while it is used and when it is thrown out. A responsible consumer thinks about all three.
points: Choosing: pick the best energy class you can afford and the correct size, and prefer repairable, durable appliances with eco and low-water programmes and little packaging.
Using: run full loads, use eco and short cycles and lower temperatures, switch off standby, defrost freezers, and do not leave fridge doors open, because each wastes energy.
Maintaining: descale and maintain appliances so that they keep working efficiently.
Disposing: repair, sell or donate an appliance while it still works, so it is not wasted.
Maintaining also helps because limescale and ice build-up make an appliance work harder and use more energy.

Under the European Union (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) Regulations 2014, a retailer must take back an old appliance of similar type free of charge, one for one, when a new one is bought, so old appliances do not end up in landfill.
Collection is on delivery if notice was given, and larger shops must accept very small items without a purchase.
Electrical waste can also go to a civic amenity site. Never put it in the household bin, which the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol warns.
notes.tip: Answer in three parts: choose efficient and correctly sized, use full loads and eco settings, and dispose through take-back or a civic amenity site.

notes.b: A washing machine shows how the selection criteria apply to a large appliance, where cost, efficiency, size and installation all matter.
points: Capacity: the drum size, stated in kilograms of dry laundry, should match the number of people in the household.
Spin speed, measured in revolutions per minute (rpm), affects how dry clothes are after washing and so how much drying is needed.
Eco and low-temperature programmes reduce water and energy use, and the energy label shows the rating for the model.
Installation needs: a water supply and drain, a suitable power point, and a level floor must all be available where the machine is placed.

notes.b: A kettle shows how the criteria apply to a small appliance, where capacity, cleaning and safety features matter most.
points: Capacity is stated in litres; buy a kettle that holds the amount the household needs, not more, because heating extra water wastes energy.
A concealed element in the base is easier to clean than an exposed element, where limescale collects.
Automatic cut-off switches the kettle off when the water boils, and boil-dry protection switches it off if the water level is too low.

keyTerms.definition: The ongoing cost of using an appliance, mainly the electricity or water it consumes over its life.
A label that rates an appliance's energy efficiency from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient) and gives its annual energy use.
The unit of energy used on energy labels, equal to the energy used by a 1 kW appliance running for one hour.
A written promise by the manufacturer or seller to repair or replace a product that is faulty within a stated period.
Support given after a purchase, including repair, servicing and the supply of spare parts.
The amount an appliance can hold or process in one use, such as litres of food or kilograms of laundry.
A mark showing that a product meets the health, safety and environmental requirements of the European Union.
A safety design in which the live parts are insulated from the user by two separate layers, so the appliance needs no earth connection.
A rating from one to four stars that shows the storage temperature and storage time of a frozen-food compartment.
A safety feature that switches off a kettle's element when the water level is too low.

factCards.term: Four appliance types that display an A to G efficiency rating
factCards.definition: Refrigerators and freezers, washing machines, tumble dryers and dishwashers.
The compartment holds food at −18°C to −25°C for up to one year, and fresh food can be frozen in it.

factCards.term: Information given on the A to G efficiency scale for a fridge-freezer
factCards.definition: The A to G efficiency class, annual energy use in kWh, noise in decibels, and fresh-food and frozen-food capacity in litres.

factCards.term: Three independent sources of consumer information
factCards.definition: Consumer magazines and websites that test products, Citizens Information and the CCPC.

factCards.term: Two safety marks on an appliance
factCards.definition: The CE mark shows compliance with EU requirements; the double insulation symbol shows two layers of insulation and no need for an earth connection.

factCards.term: Four criteria for selecting a large appliance
factCards.definition: Initial cost, running cost, size and space available, and guarantee with after-sales service.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways in which the EU energy label helps a buyer choose between appliances.
questions.model: Any two, each explained. The A to G scale allows buyers to compare the energy efficiency of different models at a glance, and an A-rated appliance is the cheapest to run and does least harm to the environment. The annual kWh figure lets buyers estimate running cost before purchase. The noise rating and the capacity figures allow buyers to choose a quieter model or one that suits household size.

questions.prompt: Describe how a household should select a large appliance for a family home, covering the selection criteria, the design features to look for and the sources of consumer information it should use.
questions.model: Selection criteria: initial cost, running cost from the energy label, size and space, capacity to suit family size, brand reliability, guarantee and after-sales service, and payment method with the total cost of any credit. Design: sturdy construction and durable materials, easy-to-read controls, smooth and removable parts for cleaning, safe features such as cut-outs and interlocks, and weight and handles suited to the user. Quality and safety: CE mark and double insulation symbol where relevant. Consumer information: independent magazines such as Consumer Choice, Citizens Information and the CCPC, energy labels and product packaging, manufacturers' leaflets used with caution, and reviews read critically. Comparing at least two models against these criteria allows the household to choose the best value.
